headline: These are not weakly-sourced rows. 40 of them are SOMEBODY ELSE'S RESEARCH filed under the wrong candidate, and the misassignments chain: Mike Collins (GA,R) -> Janak Joshi (CO,R) -> Alex Vindman (FL,D) -> David Roth (ID,D) -> Zach Wahls (IA,D), with Mike Collins also landing on Angie Nixon (FL,D).
the_lesson: ONLY 19 OF THE 40 CONTAMINATED ROWS WERE EVER IN A QUEUE. The generic-source detector asks "is this a generic profile page?", so it can only see contamination that happens to arrive on a generic-looking URL. A BORROWED CAMPAIGN WEBSITE IS THE MOST SPECIFIC-LOOKING SOURCE THERE IS: ten of Zach Wahls's eleven Season 1 rows cite rothforidaho.org and score perfectly clean, and only 2 of his 12 rows reached the queue. Janak Joshi, every one of whose twelve rows is Mike Collins's research, was in NO queue at all — he was found by probing, not by sorting. The repair unit is the PERSON, not the key.
method: Every cited page fetched and read, flattened to a single line first, and every probe run with a CONTROL TERM so an absence is evidence and not a claim about the method. (A control term is exactly what stopped a false "the Strengthening Public Schools Act does not exist" finding: the GovTrack browse endpoint is JS-rendered and returned 0 hits for "Equality Act" too.)

Every roll-call claim verified against the Clerk of the House XML, parsing the OVERALL <totals-by-vote> block — <totals-by-party> comes FIRST in the file — and checking the per-member tally equals the declared totals before reading anyone's vote. The sheet distinguishes Wilson (FL) from Wilson (SC) and Williams (GA) from Williams (TX) and (NY); both were checked on every vote.
Identity checked against the database's own records (office title, party, race candidacy), not against the reasoning's self-description.
